Our results show that simply training a relational machine learning model using existing evaluation metrics does not significantly improve the accuracy over simpler models. However, the models perform better when tested with different evaluation metrics and on various data sets. Our findings also indicate that the performance of these models varies greatly depending on the specific task and that there is a need for more systematic evaluation of relational machine learning models in pharmacology.

The work presented in this paper builds upon a series of research efforts that saw significant improvements to the Young integral's properties, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of rough paths. Specifically, this paper establishes an upper bound for the norm of the Young integral when the rough path norm is constrained within a specific condition, allowing for the extension of bounded linear operators to the Young integral's domain. This advancement relies heavily on the work of Bales, Rastegari, and Weisfelter, which provided necessary and sufficient conditions for the Young integral's convergence.

The disparity in data connectivity, or varying connectivity patterns, represents a significant obstacle in the process of developing machine learning models from dispersed data. A centralization-based approach falls short due to excessive necessary communications for data exchange. Our research introduces a random walk-inspired algorithm to tackle this challenge. The basic idea is to employ a distributed voting system where data samples, tied to individuals within a network, cast votes for the parameters of a learning model. The model's parameters are updated locally on each user based on the outcome of this voting process. The algorithm leverages the network's structure and learns the model in a decentralized manner. We establish an explicit bound for the cumulative squared error of the learned model and demonstrate its infinite-time counterpart through a theoretical analysis. Additionally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm and evaluate its effectiveness across various real-world scenarios.

Inertial wave turbulence, resulting from unstable rotating fluids, has been an object of study for various rotating systems. Recent experiments conducted in the Madouille facility have observed the development of inertial wave turbulence in a rotating cylindrical tank filled with airless water. The frequency spectrum of these waves showed a scaling relationship of $k^{-3/2}$, verifying the predictions made by L. N. Howard in the 1960s. The study also confirms the existence of an energy cascade in inertial wave turbulence, allowing for the determination of the exact time-dependent energy spectrum $E(k,t)$ and the inertial wave turbulence time scale $t_i = \omega_k^{-1} (E(k)/\eta k^2)^{1/3}$.

Mental health disorders exert a significant influence on crime rates, with approximately 25% of prisoners suffering from a mental health condition. However, the relationship between mental health and crime is intricate, involving multiple factors at play. While some mental health conditions increase the likelihood of engaging in crime, others have no link with crime rates. Furthermore, mental health treatment can decrease crime recidivism. To determine which types of crimes are influenced by mental health, we developed a multi-label crime classification system that incorporates mental health information. This system prioritizes crimes that are influenced by mental health, reducing recidivism. By integrating mental health data into the classification process, our results show improvements in crime prediction accuracy. Additionally, our approach highlights significant reductions in crime recidivism in areas with effective mental health treatments.

A widely adopted semi-supervised learning approach for medical image segmentation involves using interpolation-based mixing. This technique has been effectively implemented in various methods such as SimpleNN, PCCNN, and AdvNN. Despite its success, there is a lack of understanding about why this approach is effective. In this study, we analyze SimpleNN by comparing its performance with several alternatives, demonstrating that its reliability is no accident. We also examine the implications of its reliability on the segmentation process, as well as propose a theoretical explanation for its success. Additionally, we explore the notion that this method serves as a form of regularization for the network, which we validate through an abstraction analysis. To further enhance its performance, we propose modifying the interpolation formula to incorporate additional factors, which we evaluate through comparative studies. Our proposed changes prioritize data compliance and introduce a distance metric that promotes more precise predictions.

To address emerging challenges at the Large Hadron Collider, the Compact Muon Solenoid is undergoing significant upgrades. It will install a high-luminosity upgrade and a quartet of very compact, dual-layer forward electromagnetic converters called FEX, which require an advanced toplevel trigger system. This system, consisting of four identical modules, will need to process raw data at an expected 12.5 Tbps, and make rapid firing decisions within 400 ns. We have developed the jet FEX TTP system, utilizing a custom 16-bit link that achieves approximately 6.4 GHz in data transfer, and up to 1.5 W per link in power per 2.4 V voltage supply, and have also built a 4-module quartet prototype. This prototype, comprising 48 links, has demonstrated a link alloneserial pattern transfer rate of 6.4 GeV/s, and a minimum link threshold of 0.5 GeV/s, along with quad-module operation at 3.2 GeV/s. Additionally, the quartet prototype has successfully operated behind the CMS global trigger prototype during 2018 summer beam tests.

Articulated Neural Rendering introduces a comprehensive approach to rendering complex objects with dynamic movements and subtle deformations. By combining element-wise and compounded rendering functions, ANR achieves a balance between model simplicity and high-quality visuals. ANR operates within a neural network framework, allowing it to infer both object poses and subtle deformations from raw image data, ultimately generating realistic images of the object in question. When trained in an supervised manner on extensive datasets, ANR exhibits remarkable capabilities in producing accurate representations of objects with dynamic movements and shape transformations, even when optimized for compact pose parameter representations.

We introduce a new method to describe the local atomic structure within a specific distance of a given atom in a solid, using graph neural networks to evaluate the unique atomic configuration. This approach defines a quantity called local atomic configuration stability (LAGs) to assess the stability of local atomic structures in metals, especially near topological defects. We used this method to analyze and visualize local atomic configurations around/heal holes in platinum and iridium alloys, revealing diverse structures that correspond to those found in the bulk solid. Notably, we discovered that certain local atomic structures associated with honeycomb structures in platinum and iridium alloys are more stable than previously thought and can withstand high energies. These findings demonstrate the value of using graph neural networks to model complex local atomic structures and provide a framework for further exploration of defect physics in metals.

This paper explores the concept of weak convergence in relation to estimating function parameters, specifically conditions that ensure the consistency of a specific estimation method. We provide an analysis of a general estimation strategy that utilizes an estimate of a parameter $\theta_0$ to estimate a function $g(\theta_0)$, and establish the required conditions for this estimation strategy to be consistent when using the nearest neighbor regression estimator. We demonstrate that these conditions are akin to those necessary for the direct estimation of $g(\theta_0)$.

Evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning methods for knowledge tracing remains a difficulty due to the model's ability to adapt to previous interactions. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that student and teacher interactions often have varying qualities, making it hard to determine the relationship between traces. A common approach to addressing this challenge is by assuming that the data is sorted by quality, but this assumption is often violated in practice. Given the difficulties associated with evaluating knowledge tracing methods through comparison to existing approaches, we believe that a more effective evaluation strategy is by comparing a model's performance to a simple baseline that predicts future successes or failures based on previous interactions. This evaluation strategy is designed to be fair to all models being compared and can be applied to various knowledge tracing settings. When tested on three publicly available knowledge tracing datasets, our proposed evaluation strategy yields results that indicate a more accurate assessment of the performance of deep learning models for knowledge tracing.

We examine the relationship between being surjective and having a closed graph for a specific class of second-order elliptic differential operators acting on smooth functions, where the coefficient depends only on one variable. Our study extends beyond single-variable operators, also considering those whose coefficients are periodic in one variable and smooth in the others. In this expanded context, we establish that an operator's surjectivity follows directly from its closed graph property. Additionally, we explore connections to existence results for boundary value problems.

Since its introduction at the PxTP workshop, the veriT proof format has undergone significant enhancements and has gained popularity among various SAT and SMT solvers. This survey provides an in-depth analysis of the veriT proof format, detailing its gradual advancements and highlighting the benefits they offer, particularly in deepening the connection between logical reasoning and computational verification.

FedBuff is a newly proposed private, scalable, and adaptable federated learning version of the FedAvg algorithm. FedBuff achieves this by limiting each participant's updated vector to a random sampling and reducing the number of participants whose data is used for updating the global average by applying a histogram-based method. In contrast to FedProx, FedBuff avoids adding excess noise to the updates by participants and instead allows the global average to be updated with a limited subset of participants' updates. This characteristic of FedBuff allows it to provide robust privacy protection to participants during the adaptation process. It's also shown that, under specific conditions, the convergence rate of FedBuff can be as high as O(1/T) in terms of expected square loss.

The success of speech recognition systems often relies on extensive data fine-tuning using a large in-domain training set. Yet, certain applications like cross-language transfers may benefit from a different approach due to limited resources and significant lexical differences. In our experiments, we found that a deep learning-based architecture can achieve notable results with minimal data when trained on out-of-domain datasets, specifically when using a technique called domain mask augmentation to simulate in-domain conditions. We used a multilingual encoder with a language-specific tokenizer and two datasets to compare the effectiveness of transfer learning: the cross-language transfer of speech recognition, using out-of-domain datasets in place of in-domain datasets, and the recognition of mispronunciations, using a small in-domain dataset. Our results show that this method can significantly reduce the need for data fine-tuning and alleviate the requirement for extensive datasets, especially when transferring between languages with limited similarity and correcting mispronunciations with limited in-domain data.

The development of novel node embedding techniques relies on experimental comparison, but a standardized evaluation method is missing. To address this challenge, we introduce a new approach for exponential achievement and a sampling strategy for fair comparison, which can be applied to various graph classification tasks. Additionally, we provide an open-source framework that incorporates both the new evaluation method and strategies, as well as commonly used node embedding techniques, and demonstrates their practical applications through explicit implementation and testing on multiple datasets. The code is available online for further research community reference.

Our current understanding of hadron spectroscopy is refined through the study of rare $B$-meson decays, specifically looking at final states that involve multiple particles. By analyzing 480 billion $B$-meson events collected with the LHCb detector, this research focuses on two rare processes: $B^+\to K^+ K_S K_S$ and $B^0\to K^0 \bar{K}^{0} \pi^0$. Initial findings revealed a broad structure in the $B^+\to K^+ K_S K_S$ spectrum resulting from a $J^P=0^-$ wave, while this study aims to explore the relationship between that wave and the reported structure in the $B^0\to K^0 \bar{K}^{0} \pi^0$ spectrum, specifically the $K^0 \bar{K}^{0}$ pair. Utilizing 9.2 fb^-1 of data from the LHCb detector at the CERN, this research utilizes an amplitude analysis to identify and characterize the $B^0\to (K^0 \bar{K}^{0}) \pi^0$ structure, further understanding the $B^+\to K^+ K_S K_S$ structure, and comparing the two to validate quantum chromodynamics. The findings support the predicted quark composition of the $B^0\to (K^0 \bar{K

Recent studies suggest that Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) in a specific range could account for all dark matter. To further explore this concept, researchers updated existing mechanisms for producing PBHs and examined their potential to form a majority of dark matter. The updated scenarios, which include a novel approach where a sound wave produces a rarefied region, were used in a simplified model to simulate PBH creation. The simulations were then combined with an explanation of how these PBHs would maintain their stability in various environments. There is a particular range of PBH masses, from $10^{17}$ grams to 10 times the mass of the sun, for which the production rate in the updated scenarios meets the needs to constitute 50% of all dark matter. However, to explain all of dark matter, the ideal PBH mass would be around $10^{20}$ grams. The existing mechanisms for producing PBHs, which involve the collision of two objects such as stars or black holes, produce a limited quantity of PBHs regardless of their mass. In contrast, the sound wave mechanism results in a nearly linear relationship between the production rate of PBHs and their mass.

To compensate for the nonlinearities in sensing force through series elastic actuators and the inaccuracies inherent in sensor measurements, a novel algorithm known as Nested Integration with Bias Correction has been developed. This method, centered on utilizing multiple simultaneous force measurements to estimate the actual applied force, has been shown to effectively counter both linear and nonlinear system forces as well as accurately measure both small and large forces. The algorithm's performance was evaluated using a simplified mathematical model and confirmed through practical testing with a actual SEFA setup. The results indicate that the algorithm is capable of providing accurate measurements even in presence of significant stiffness nonlinearity and sensor errors, and is particularly efficient with only two samples required per second.

A distinctive pattern of break-up, characterized by the progressive enlargement of gaps between particles, is observed in raft-like collections of solid particles suspended in a viscous fluid, when the raft is subjected to an externally applied tension. This phenomenon occurs before the raft breaks into individual particles. We have developed a theoretical model to describe the time it takes for two adjacent particles to separate by a certain distance in the raft by comparing the rates of two opposing forces: the tendency of particles to stick together and the influence of the surrounding fluid expanding the raft. Our theoretical predictions align with experimental data and provide further insight into the competition between these two forces as the raft is stretched.

This study examines the behavior of multicomponent complex scalar fields under lattice scale transformation, focusing on theories that exhibit distinct phase shifts during the renormalization-group flow. Inspired by the Wilsonian perspective, we investigate whether Lattice Field Theory can preserve the renormalization group's fundamental principles, specifically near fixed points and non-trivial phase transitions. By exploring a range of models featuring two or more complex scalar fields, we observe that certain phase transitions in these models can be mapped to the corresponding phases found in single complex scalar field theories. Additionally, we find that certain deep-infrared asymptotes, corresponding to fully condensed phases, can be understood through the lens of effective potential. Furthermore, we observe that certain shallow-infrared limits can be described by marginally unstable operators, which can be connected to the underlying continuum theory's spectrum.

Deep reinforcement learning methods have been successful in solving complex problems, but they face challenges when applied to time-critical and high-stability tasks due to their slow learning processes. Underwater glider navigation is such a task that is difficult to stabilize because of its slow speed and large operational area. To accelerate the learning process, a new algorithm called SPGP-SARSA was developed, combining a value function estimator utilizing sparse geometric projection with policy iteration. In SPGP-SARSA, the estimator helps evaluate states more efficiently during policy iteration. In testing the algorithm, a underwater glider simulation was used with unstable and coherent current patterns. The results showed that SPGP-SARSA can quickly learn to stabilize the glider in flowing waters and achieve optimal energy efficiency when navigating between pre-determined destinations. The method demonstrated superior performance in evaluating states during policy iteration, with a significant reduction in reward evaluation time. On average, SPGP-SARSA evaluated a state's reward 7.5 times faster than the baseline algorithm.

We explore the concept of sorting networks with various arities and networks that can sort any permutation of numbers across different depths. We demonstrate that with depth 4, binary sorting networks are sufficient, but this minimal arity increases with deeper networks: 3 with depth 1, 3 with depth 2, 4 with depth 3, and 5 with depth greater than 3. We also provide a method to construct balanced sorting networks for any arity and depth greater than 1, and show that this construction sort networks with the fewest gates for certain small inputs and depths. However, we then prove that for depths greater than 2, sorting networks can be asymptotically tight, with a minimal arity of almost n times a constant for large input sizes n.

Using the relativistic theory of multicomponent fluids, we derive solutions for stars composed of two fluids with the same symmetry as those in the single-fluid model. By establishing a relationship between the metrics of single-fluid and multi-fluid solutions, we demonstrate that the latter can be obtained from the former through specific transformations. Additionally, we find that multi-fluid solutions are a necessary aspect of relativistic theory. This is evident in the form of a constraint on single-fluid solutions, which the multi-fluid solutions must satisfy. This constraint takes the form of an equation of state for the single fluid, where the properties of the individual fluids are interlinked. Consequently, a relativistic single-fluid model cannot have an equation of state that depends on both density and pressure simultaneously. Instead, the equation of state for the single fluid must be determined explicitly before being used in computations. This finding is a significant aspect of the theory of multicomponent fluids.

We performed high-resolution N-body simulations of near-barred galaxies to study bar formation, using a novel integration method that maintains exact preservation of angular momentum. Our models featured massive, collisionally relaxed, stellar systems, consistent with observed galactic disks, and incorporated an advanced force calculation technique that tightly controlled force errors. Following a cooling phase, during which the disk's scale length decreased, and a phase of bar formation, we analyzed the results, finding that the bar's formation was accelerated, and its speed of formation correlated with the disk's scale length, to a power of two over one.

This study examines the outcome of collision between two galaxies with a high density of gas, using advanced computational modeling. The model incorporates the effect of magnetic fields on collision dynamics. The found that, due to magnetic fields, the collision results in the creation of a separate system composed of the merging galaxies, rather than a merger remnant. However, by increasing the density of gas in the model to more accurately reflect observations, the creation of magnetic field remnants is prevented, allowing the merger to create heavy elements through star formation in its galaxy.

To address the issue of severity underestimation in COVID-19 CT image analysis, this paper introduces the 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification (3DCMC) network. 3DCMC is a pioneering attempt that combines contrastive learning and mixup techniques within a cascade classification structure. By incorporating contrastive learning, 3DCMC efficiently expands the diversity of sampled hard negative examples, thereby overcoming the limitation of a small training dataset. Additionally, 3DCMC uses a balanced loss function in each cascade layer to address the issue of data imbalance. In evaluation tests, the proposed method achieved the highest severity accuracy and F-score compared to existing methods. The 3DCMC network also demonstrated robust performance on noise-corrupted COVID-19 CT images, showing great potential for severity detection tasks.

This study presents a novel method for adapting Generative Error Correction models
to new domains, building on the principle that errors can be viewed as deviations
from correct text. We utilize multi-task denoising autoencoders to capture the
error distribution and apply domain adaptation techniques to adapt the error model.
Our method involves two stages: first, we train a error distribution model that can
be applied to multiple tasks (GEC); second, when adapting the model to a new domain
(or task), we incorporate both the error model and the text generation model.
Our experiments show that this approach surpasses traditional multi-task transfer
learning methods and support our theory of error adaptation using multi-task
denoising autoencoders. Additionally, our results demonstrate that this method
achieves comparable performance to current state-of-the-art GEC models.

In October 2019, a national emergency was declared in Japan due to a significant increase in suicide rates following a major life event. To provide timely suicide rate estimates, the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) typically releases annual suicide rate data. However, usual spatial statistical methods can be problematic when applying the MHLW's practice of rounding suicide rates to the nearest five. This study proposes an alternative method for statistical inference, considering the rounding as measurement error, to maintain the integrity of suicide rates and previous mapping practices. Our research indicates that the proposed approach yields more accurate estimates and maintains visible geographic patterns. To demonstrate the method's effectiveness, we conducted a comparative analysis using pre and post-data scenarios, and the results showed the proposed method outperformed standard methods. Notably, the proposed approach produced more reliable results even with the MHLW's rounding policy in place, and is recommended for its superior performance.

GdInO3 is a p-type semiconducting material that has been investigated for its potential to reduce NOx emissions. However, there is a lack of data on its physical properties. A study presents GdInO3's atomic and lattice structures as derived from simulated XAS and XRD data, showing that Gd3+ ions form a hexagonal lattice while also influencing the In5+ ions around them. These structures are compared to those of related materials, and the results are used to inform a discussion on the material's electrical properties. Additionally, a method is demonstrated to extract effective Bader charges from XAS spectra, and this technique is applied to analyze the charging behavior in GdInO3.

The Round-Robin mechanism is a simple allocation method used in scheduling and intersection maintenance tasks. A more efficient approach exists in the form of the cut-and-choose algorithm, although both methods share the property of being approximately fair. A new research finds that the Round-Robin mechanism provides a minimum fairness guarantee of $2/3$, which is the crucial finding in this study. It also demonstrates that this mechanism has a fairness guarantee of $1-\varepsilon$ by utilizing the algorithm's $\varepsilon$-approximability. As a result, the Round-Robin mechanism can be used as a fair allocation method with a guarantee of $\varepsilon$-approximating the optimal solution.

We introduce an innovative pseudo-labeling technique for using translated versions of a single target image to label the target data. We argue that leveraging multiple translations of a single target image yields more accurate labels than relying on a single translation. Our proposed method involves averaging predictions from various translations of the target image to create a single label. We demonstrate that this approach is effective in labeling target data when the target domain data is limited. We evaluate our method on two benchmark settings – the fully supervised setting and the semi-supervised setting – and show that it achieves superior performance compared to solo pseudo-labeling methods. Our model's performance is on par with the current state-of-the-art methods that utilize massive target domain data.

We undertook a detailed analysis of HII regions within the nearby galaxy UGC 8839.
Our catalog of around 2000 minutes of exposure includes over 800 HII region candidates.
We used a modified version of the SINGDR2 HII region selection algorithm to identify 1212 high confidence HII regions, of which 779 were selected as low confidence candidates.
Our final data consists of 1212 HII regions with accurate radial distances from the center of the galaxy, ranging from 0.5 to 21.7 kpc, and varying declinations between 18.5° and 41.5°.
We identified 7 well-isolated ring features and compared them to 7 less defined ring features and 2 outer ring features and bar structures to understand their spatial distribution and velocities using the Tully-Fisher relation.
We found that the galaxy's inner star formation regions within 0.5 kpc are within the central bulge, and from 0.5 to 14.2 kpc, HII regions are organized in 7 circular orbits.
We discovered that 6 of these orbits share the same stellar patterns observed in other galaxies like M101 and UGC 12945, whereas the 7th orbit is unique to UGC 8839.
We also found that the galaxy's inner regions within 0.5 kpc have the highest star formation rates compared to the outer regions.

Researchers suggest that a novel instrument, the paleo-detector, can identify the interaction between dark matter and nucleons at low mass scales, possibly in the range of 100-1000 GeV. This could provide a significant breakthrough, as this range is currently difficult to study with other experiments. By analyzing the sensitivity of paleo-detectors in a range where other experiments are less effective, scientists can potentially gain valuable insights into dark matter properties. However, this would require very sensitive detectors that can detect minimal interactions between dark matter and nucleons, which is based on analytical models of such interactions. Nonetheless, researchers are exploring the potential of paleo-detectors to contribute to the understanding of dark matter, which is a major mystery in physics.

Modern databases managing sensitive information like healthcare records often rely on encryption, protecting data accessibility while limiting access to update history information. Recent research has demonstrated the feasibility of releasing encrypted update history data while complying with differential privacy standards. However, current methodologies primarily focus on certain types of updates, such as insertions and deletions. A new framework, titled DPUpdate, is introduced to address updates of varying kinds, including additions, deletions, and modifications, while ensuring differential privacy is maintained. DPUpdate provides a standardized interface for database management systems to integrate with privacy-enhancing tools and has been successfully tested on post-encryption databases, showcasing its effectiveness.

We've developed a novel approach to analyzing feature importance within machine learning models, drawing from the field of constraint satisfaction. This method, centered on Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores, pinpoints specific model variables that, when optimized, enable the identification of essential model features. We've observed that our approach surpasses existing techniques in both efficiency and precision. Furthermore, we've found that in several domains, including image classification, the key features revealed by our method closely align with those identified through human inspection, thus suggesting that this approach has practical application in providing actionable insights into model performance.

Recently, deep learning techniques, such as Deep Learning Based Instrument Segmentation (DLBIS), have emerged as effective solutions for the automated identification of surgical tools from video footage. However, current DLBIS approaches are primarily focused on developing sophisticated models rather than clarifying the internal mechanics of these networks. In an effort to achieve a transparent and trustworthy automation process for surgical assistance, a new attention-based network called Dual decoder attention Network (DDANet) has been proposed that incorporates a detailed analysis of each component's function. By incorporating a comparison with seven leading DLBIS models, our results demonstrate that DDANet achieves superior performance, with an average score of 78.95% across four challenging evaluation datasets. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that each component of DDANet contributes significantly to its overall performance, with the inclusion of each attention mechanism resulting in a substantial improvement in model accuracy.

In the field of unsupervised ReID, our proposed contrastive learning method is both effective and efficient. Although contrastive learning methods are commonly used for unsupervised ReID, they often rely on time-consuming and labor-intensive data preparation. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel, self-supervised contrastive learning approach called Self-Contrastive ReID. This method involves first extracting visual features from mobile ReID models, and then developing a  memory-based sample contrastive learning approach to improve the feature's cross-domain matching performance. We conducted extensive experiments using the MSMT1M and LumoRe datasets, and our results show significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art unsupervised ReID methods. Our work contributes to the development of efficient self-supervised contrastive learning methods for ReID.

This study presents a novel, robust, and efficient GARCH-based approach for computing Value-at-Risk. The proposed model, tailored for financial time series data, builds on the APGARCH model and incorporates elements of the Bayesian information criterion and the non-linear least squares method. This leads to a simplified structure with fewer parameters and better performance than the original GARCH-FM model. The research compares the proposed model to traditional GARCH models, GARCH-FM and other alternative methodologies, for forecasting Var and Expected Shortfall through experimental analysis. The results show that the proposed model achieves more accurate Var forecasts and comparable performance to the best methods for Expected Shortfall, outperforming other models in some cases. The associated source code is available online.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) use collaborative resources from hundreds of radio telescopes around the world to evaluate a vast dataset for signs of neutron star motions influenced by gravitational waves. Due to the enormous scale of this data, analyzing PTA parameters with a grid-based approach is impractical, prompting the development of various sampling algorithms to selectively evaluate the most promising areas. In this study, we directly compared traditional methods, including the PTAs-specific particle swarm optimisation and a simple random sampling algorithm, in relation to their ability to identify potential gravitational wave signals. Our findings suggest that the basic random sampling algorithm performs comparably to more complex methods, offering a severely reduced computational requirement with comparable detection performance. This finding could provide cost-effective options for computational resources in future PTA experiments, particularly those involving the direct comparison of different sampling strategies.

This study examines the relationships between quark masses in different flavor combinations and the properties of pions, using lattice QCD simulations with a 0.04 to 0.18 GeV range of quark mass variations. Our findings indicate significant connections between the $m_s/m_d$ ratio and the pion decay constant, as well as between the $m_c/m_s$ ratio and the pion glue content. Conversely, we did not observe a clear connection between the $m_c/m_s$ ratio and the pion distribution amplitude. Our research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between quark mass variations and pion properties, which is crucial for precise calculations of direct CP violation in kaon decays.

Even from a distance, the classical T Tauri star DX Cha seems to be in a state of extreme activity, with its sun-shaped size varying significantly and unusual orbital patterns. Located about 400 light years from Earth, DX Cha exhibits extreme variability in its accretion rates, which is unlike anything observed before. This exceptional variability has a profound effect on our understanding of T Tauri star disks, which are now shown to evolve rapidly. A team of astronomers used the ESPRESSo spectrograph at the La Silla Observatory to analyze DX Cha's spectrum, which revealed the presence of a redshifted water vapor absorption band associated with high-speed winds. The observation of this absorption band provided an indicator of the star's mass accretion rate. Additionally, the analysis of DX Cha's spectrum revealed the presence of a recently discovered type of wind pattern, known as the radial-burnt model, which is characterized by winds that are burned by energy released during the star-disk interaction. The model also predicts the presence of a second type of wind pattern, which could result in the burn of radial winds that reach the star's surface. However, DX Cha's spectrum did not display this second type of wind pattern. The analysis also revealed that DX Cha's wind patterns are similar to those of another T Tauri star, LkCa 15, which has the same size and orbital period. However, DX Cha's wind patterns are more active, with higher mass accretion

People generally support using luck to allocate wealth, but the underlying conditions that steer this opinion vary significantly. In one scenario, known as the difference principle, opportunities are split into luck-based and effort-based categories, and the fair distribution of wealth is determined by these factors. In another scenario, known as the luck egalitarianism, the primary aim is to compensate individuals for bad luck that directly affects their income. A theoretical analysis of these conditions reveals that, in certain situations, both principles can produce the same results, while in other situations, they can yield distinct outcomes. In such cases, public opinion may side with the difference principle, whereas in other circumstances, public opinion may support luck egalitarianism. A survey involving over 1,000 respondents was used to test these predictions, and the results show that people's preferences for these principles do differ, especially in scenarios that parallel the theoretical conditions. In these scenarios, people on average prefer the difference principle in situations where opportunities are divided between luck and effort, and they prefer luck egalitarianism in scenarios where luck directly affects income.

This paper delves into the connection between the Euler characteristics of certain geometric objects called stable maps, and their associated quantum K-invariants in the context of the mirror conjecture. By utilizing a technique called degeneration, we establish a relationship between these Euler characteristics and the quantum K-invariants on a larger space that includes the original space as a component. We then apply this relationship to derive formulas for certain Euler characteristics by setting specific parameters in the quantum K-invariants. As a result, we verify the mirror conjecture for one particular situation, and also obtain a related geometric formula that was previously unknown. Another area we explore is the connection between stable maps and Chow groups, particularly how certain elements in the Chow groups of smooth varieties relate to the quantum K-invariants through a chain of correspondences.

Data debugging, a newly emerging field, focuses on efficiently identifying and correcting errors in machine learning pipelines. In contrast to traditional approaches which involve comprehending the entire dataset, we introduce DataScope, an innovative framework enhancing data debugging efficiency by narrowing down problematic data samples. DataScope's lightweight design allows it to detect anomalies, locate data errors, and even provide explicit corrections without needing the entire dataset. Through both theoretical and practical validation, we demonstrate DataScope's effectiveness in data debugging. Additionally, our work lays the groundwork for future data debugging research and showcases the practical applicability of DataScope in real-world scenarios.

The search for millisecond pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries within 20 kpc of the Sun has led to the detection of 11 new radio sources within the cores of globular clusters.  Of these, 7 are low-frequency radio luminosities that are characteristic of neutron star X-ray binaries, while 4 others exhibit radio properties similar to millisecond pulsars.  The research involves a radio frequency band from 1.4 to 5.0 GHz and was conducted with the 100-m Green Bank Telescope, with the majority of the observations taking place between September 2014 and July 2018 as part of the FIRST Survey second data release.  To differentiate pulsars from other celestial sources, a thorough examination was performed across three frequency bands and resulted in the discovery of 11 new pulsars, with ten of them being previously unknown.  Eight of the newly found pulsars are binary systems with their corresponding eccentric orbits, while three others show the signature of a millisecond spin period.  One of these new pulsars, with a spin period of approximately 1.6 milliseconds, was found in the Terzan 2 cluster and may be linked to the X-ray source Terzan 2 X3.

When conducting graph data analysis, a significant challenge arises when reconstructing hypergraphs from their projections, especially given the vast number of possible combinations. This issue becomes even more daunting when the projections are limited, as is often the case in many applications. This study proposes a novel approach to addressing this problem by linking a small, low-density subgraph to a large, dense hypergraph projection. This approach not only provides a feasible solution to the reconstruction problem but also offers a valuable framework for exploring other types of structured graphs. This framework can be utilized in a parameter-free manner that adapts to the characteristics of the target data and is adaptable to various types of structured graphs, such as those with specific node and edge patterns. This is achieved through the incorporation of graph embeddings that capture distinct patterns and incorporate a low-dimensional latent variable that distingu al between nodes within the same hypergraph. This leads to a flexible energy minimization algorithm that can be applied in a parameter-free manner and adapts to different types of structured graphs, such as those with specific node and edge patterns. This method can be utilized in a parameter-free manner that adapts to the characteristics of the target data. This is demonstrated through the reconstruction of small-world hypergraphs and the detection of fractures in oil reservoirs.

The emission direction from lasers is considered uniform until it reaches a certain point, beyond which the direction becomes less settled and eventually sticks to a particular emission path. This behavior is analyzed by introducing the divergence angle, which is linked to the direction-emitting pattern from lasers. It is observed that the divergence angle remains consistent across different emission modes and even mirrors. Moreover, it is seen that the minimum divergence angle is linked to the size of the laser and can be interpreted through the diffraction limit.

We investigate the interaction between coherent light and a group of atoms for which a specific frequency correlation is altered by an external classical force, often referred to as speaker light. We examine the impact on the scattering of light over a broad range of conditions, from situations where the light is strongly connected to atoms, to cases where the light behaves independently of atom behavior, and even in scenarios where the classical force has significant, but not total, control. We focus on understanding two aspects: a longer-lasting correlation between two types of light, and a shorter-lasting correlation between the same type of light observed from two different locations. We find that the classical force's level of control directly affects the type of light produced, and that this is more apparent in the longer-lasting correlation. Additionally, the fact that the classical force can have significant, but not total, control allows for the direct observation of the atoms' quantum behavior, which would otherwise be masked.

Offline learning for multiple agents can be a complex task due to the lack of coordinated data availability. In this work, we're addressing this challenge with a novel approach called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT), which restructures existing data into a unified representation and enables individual agents to learn from it. Our proposed method involves two key components: first, we transform the data into a form that captures the shared knowledge by mapping each agent's unique state and action space into a common domain; second, we employ a technique called inverse dynamics modeling to model each agent's dynamics and learn a policy that can be applied to the shared representation. This method allows each agent to learn from the combined data of all agents, even when working independently. We tested SIT on offline multi-agent learning scenarios and found it to be an effective approach.

A new method has been introduced for accurate image registration, based on Convolutional Neural Networks, that bypasses traditional intensity-based optimization techniques. This approach leverages contrast information present in raw image data to achieve more precise alignment, as demonstrated in an experiment involving magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography image pairs, resulting in a model capable of producing robust and efficient registrations. Compared to conventional methods, this approach showed a notable improvement in initial misalignment tolerance, as evidenced by results from multiple testing scenarios. Additionally, the model's performance was found to be highly consistent and capable of producing high-quality registrations even in the presence of moderate motion, paving the way for its potential application in medical image registration scenarios.

We investigate how single-particle entanglement affects steering in complex quantum systems consisting of multiple particles, building on previous research that demonstrated single-particle entanglement can generate nonlocal phenomena in single-photon systems. Utilizing a Gaussian state of two modes with single-particle entanglement as a model, we find that partial entanglement in this state can lead to strong steering, and we analyze how this behaves under linear transformations such as beam splitter and Kerr interactions. Our findings also indicate that partial entanglement in this state results in robust steering in lossy channels, particularly in scenarios where one mode experiences high loss, revealing an unexpected connection between single-particle entanglement and efficient information acquisition in quantum channels.

The rising popularity of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has created a pressing need to enhance road safety, driven by the widespread use of connected and automated vehicles. IoVs' complex communication networks pose significant security challenges, primarily centered on the exposure of sensitive information such as location details and navigation paths. A prominent solution to address these concerns is Blockchain technology, given its proven track record in maintaining data privacy and integrity across various networks. Nevertheless, the implementation of Blockchain in IoVs raises computational efficiency concerns, given the inherent time-consuming process of achieving consensus. In response to this challenge, this study proposes a novel Blockchain-based data security scheme for IoVs, leveraging a unique hybrid architecture that combines the benefits of Leverage Rich Clubs and Bet-and-Win models to yield improved energy efficiency and reduced latency. In doing so, the proposed scheme demonstrates superior performance compared to existing Blockchain-based data security solutions for IoVs.

Our research offers a comprehensive framework for understanding how novae like V392 Persei explode, based on the properties of the system. V392 Persei, which he exploded in 2014, is a satellite nova that was observed to be in an exceptional state of explosion. Our team used the MAXI, Swift, and Kepler observations, which showed that the explosion was highly luminous and brief, lasting about 27 days. During this time, the system accumulated a significant amount of material on its companion star, which resulted in a substantial increase in X-ray radiation. Our analysis indicates that the explosion affected the system's accretion state, which was in a high-sweep rate condition due to the large amount of material accumulated on the companion star. However, our research indicates that the system's orbital period is shorter than previously estimated and that the white dwarf has a high mass. Our study also reveals that the explosion's exceptional duration can be attributed to the system's high mass and its minimal pre-outburst activity.

To assess the efficacy of individual quantum gates, we utilize a highly entangled resource, the toric code, which is also valuable for fault-tolerant quantum computing. We develop an efficient, sequential method to accurately measure the average entanglement of this resource over a two-dimensional lattice site. This approach builds upon previous work by incorporating a vast amount of entanglement, obtained through the application of single-qubit gates following a predetermined pattern. We demonstrate that our methodful implementation can exceed 99% of the measured average entanglement when compared to a perfectly measured ideal scenario. Furthermore, we successfully execute our protocol on a minimum of 5 integrated qubits located on the edge of a 3D cubic structure, incorporated within a fault-prone environment, to evaluate the impact of gate faults on our measurement results. We found that our method can distinguish between healthy and faulty quantum gates, particularly those with specific error patterns, by analyzing the measured entanglement and corresponding parity measurements.

The proposed adaptive encoding scheme divides data points into distinct clusters based on their similarity, with the aim of minimizing uncertainty in data samples that have not been observed before. This approach results in significantly reduced pilot usage when compared to traditional clustering methods, with only 1 pilot used for every 8 times the number of cluster count. This advancement holds significant potential for optimizing resource allocation in various learning applications, with minimal computational requirements.

We investigate the behavior of a two-dimensional Dirac model with an opaque boundary, which has been coaxed into creating a gap by a nearby source, and we find that surface currents display remarkable resilience in both quantum and classical regimes. The robust nature of these surface currents is evident even in the presence of spin fluctuations and temperature, and we determine the associated Berry phase, exchange energies, and chemical potential by adopting alternative calculational methods. Furthermore, we outline the potential for observing these surface currents in silicon and germanium samples using interband electrical measurements.

This study examines the Brans-Dicke theory with a scalar gravitational field that varies according to a particular function, ensuring that photons can reach null infinity. We identify the behavior of this function at different distances from the source, from a near-field area where the Brans-Dicke parameter affects it, to the regime where it acts like a constant in the asymptotic region. We also find that the scalar field's variation follows a specific quadratic pattern with respect to the distance, which includes an adjustable coefficient influenced by the mass and energy of the source, as well as the speed of light. This coefficient represents a measure of the scalar gravitational radiation and must meet certain conditions to allow photons to escape to null infinity. We then compare our results with those of other researchers who have studied the same problem using different approaches.

Using a semi-analytical model, we investigated the merger rate of Population III binary remnants within the LIGO sensitivity range, and found this rate occurs at a density of approximately 0.4 years$^{-1}$ per cubic gigaparsec at a redshift of 0.7. These events are primarily caused by the merger of neutron stars and black holes in low-mass binary systems that form through gravitational wave emission during the Universe's cosmic structure formation. Additionally, we found that a future LIGO-generation detector with a sensitivity increase of $\sqrt{10}$ will be able to detect these events at a density of around 20 years$^{-1}$ per cubic gigaparsec within the Universe's current cosmic structure.

We discuss the design of a computer-based simulator for Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and the results of timing measurements it yielded, which proved significant in determining the sensitivity of a LaBr$_3$ (Eu$^{2+}$) based imaging detector for high-energy events. The GRB simulator's time jitter of around 87 ns surpassed typical measurements in burst detection. Using the simulator, we conducted dose-dependent tests of the detector's performance, observing that at low doses it was susceptible to fluctuations, but at higher doses it accurately identified the simulated GRBs. The simulator also enabled us to assess the effectiveness of the detector's anti-coincidence plastic scintillator, which indicated a significant reduction in false positives.

Let's denote the compact part of T_g as T_g^0 and its remaining part as T_g^1. It has been established in previous research that if g belongs to the BMOA_p space (where 1 < p < 2), then T_g^0 exists and is compact on the standard Dirichlet space H^2, while T_g^1 is not compact on H^2. This paper delves deeper, proving that for any g in BMOA_p (with 1 < p < 2), the operator T_g is compact on the weighted Dirichlet space H^2_p. Furthermore, it demonstrates the optimality of this result by showing a function g in BMOA_p, for 1 < p <= 2, such that T_g^1 is not compact on the weighted Dirichlet space H^2_p. Additionally, this paper explores the relationship between T_g and another operator, where \tilde{T_g^1} is the extension of T_g^1 to the space F^2...

The vast and ever-expanding literature comprises knowledge that evolves over time, 
wherein the development across lower levels can be inferred from the higher levels. 
The Literome Project aims to map the literature using the Conceptual Index of 
Quantitative Knowledge (KQI), a spatial framework that illustrates the flow of 
knowledge within literature. The project's goal is to provide researchers with a 
visual tool to identify areas of knowledge that require exploration. A set of 
automated techniques was developed to assign literature to KQI topics and map 
the relationships between them. The project's database now comprises over 430,000 
PubMed entries, with a subset of 24,000 annotated papers used to evaluate the 
approach. The results show a high correlation between the proposed method and 
established annotation techniques for identifying KQI topics and the strength of 
relationships between them. The project's website and database are available at 
https://www.literome.org.

In a wireless communication system, security is achieved through a process called caching, at various nodes including access points and user equipment. The overall security depends on the power allocation at these nodes. We've developed an optimization technique to determine the power allocation, caching content, and transmission strategy, ensuring overall security is maintained. This approach considers the total power available at each node and the security requirements for different messages. The optimization problem is formulated in a way that allows for solution through a process called decomposition, making it more efficient. The key advantage of this approach is that it requires less communication between nodes, thus reducing the need for inter-node coordination. The resulting problem is then solvable through a technique called sequential quadratic programming. We've also analyzed the complexity of the algorithm and its effectiveness. Through simulation, we've demonstrated the benefits of our approach, showing improved security and energy efficiency.

Quantum emitters hold promise for distributing entanglement via non-local interactions with other systems. Our analysis indicates that in networks featuring robust edge states, weakly coupled quantum emitters can be employed to create entangled states between two distinct spectral regions. We demonstrate this concept using a 1D topological model and show that even weak interactions between the emitters and the edge states can generate highly entangled states. The fidelity of these states remains robust against perturbations and decay, and can be stabilized using a feedback control method. Furthermore, we find that the same principle can be applied in 2D networks using dark states in a lattice model.

In the complex context of urban intersections, an automated vehicle equipped with connectivity can optimize its path by heuristics and optimization techniques, despite limitations imposed by traffic signals, other vehicles, and lane changes. We develop a more comprehensive method for predicting the automated vehicle's entire journey through an intersection, factoring in the influences of yellow and red signals, potential collisions, and lane changes. This method involves dividing the journey into two parts - approaching the queue and navigating through it - and applying nonlinear programming to find the most efficient path. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with a simulation of a typical urban intersection.

We introduce a new fast text-based world model called TextWorldExpress, 
which significantly boosts simulation speeds by 15-20 times and achieves 
near-original levels with only 128 bytes of state size. Our approach 
incorporates neural network-based action predictors, limited world transitions, 
and a simplified parsing engine. These innovations enable TextWorldExpress 
to support high-throughput simulations for large-scale experiments and studies.

Deep learning techniques have rapidly emerged as powerful solutions for various challenges in data analysis and signal processing, primarily fueled by the incredible effectiveness of recurrent neural networks and sub-symbolic learning strategies in extracting meaningful patterns from complex data. However, the significant computational resources required to execute these algorithms efficiently on conventional hardware have created significant barriers to their widespread adoption. In the realm of hardware design, there is a growing interest in creating dedicated accelerators for time-series prediction tasks that leverage the inherent structure of data and employed algorithms to achieve maximum performance efficiency. Existing tensor decomposed model-oriented hardware accelerators have already achieved remarkable performance levels, but there is still an unmet need for more advanced acceleration frameworks capable of handling complex hidden states and long-term dependencies inherent to certain time-series data. To address this gap, we introduce a novel FDHT-LSTM architecture that combines the efficient memory access pattern of hardware-oriented accelerators with the exceptional performance of deep learning algorithms, and for its implementation, we propose an innovative hybrid accelerator that integrates Cross-Bar memory and LSI accelerators, delivering a significant boost in performance and energy efficiency while maintaining high hardware efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that the hybrid accelerator realizes a throughput increase of up to 4.3-fold and enhances energy efficiency by up to 8.5 for the FDHT-LSTM application, underscoring the immense potential of this acceleration framework for various time-series prediction workloads.

To enhance the efficiency of NLP models by reducing the need for large labeled datasets, this study explores various data augmentation techniques, focusing on context-aware methods that understand the semantic significance of individual words within a sentence. We evaluated multiple context-aware data augmentation models, incorporating both simple and complex models, with both automatic and human-assessed evaluation metrics showing they could achieve comparable performance to models using vast amounts of labeled data, despite being fine-tuned with just a fraction of that amount. We further found that these models could successfully avoid labeling certain parts of the dataset with difficult sentences, thus effectively allocating resources across samples.

A recent hypothesis suggests that large extra dimensions could lead to a weakly coupled, stable universe. To test this, researchers studied a scenario where a scalar field is confined to a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, and interacted with a massless graviton field. By calculating the scalar's self-binding energy, they found that its effective mass is affected in a way that doesn't align with the Weak Gravity Conjecture's proposed framework. This discrepancy arises due to a phenomenon that doesn't exist in previous, four-dimensional analyses. Although the scalar remains stable, its behavior doesn't meet the conjecture's requirements, and the hypothesis needs further modification to accommodate general situations.

To simulate multiple quantum states simultaneously, our proposed approach constructs a variety of wavefunction models and tests their differences mathematically. This strategy potentially offers a more efficient way to calculate multiple ground and excited states simultaneously. Building upon this, we also develop an optimized method to minimize the number of models required, thereby enhancing the accuracy of approximate wavefunctions even in challenging scenarios. By incorporating a technique to bypass the complexity of two-electron integrals, our method can successfully handle a wide range of calculations. We validate our approach through a series of tests involving both simple systems and more complex scenarios, and it outperforms even the most advanced alternative methods in several cases.

Given a strong F-shape local ring L containing a proper, strongly F-rational local ring R, we examine the zero submodule of local cohomology modules $\ Koh_{F}(L)$. Specifically, for $i\geq 1$, we determine that $\ Koh_{F}(L)_{(i)}$ contains a non-zero submodule $\ M_{(i)}$ that maintains the strong F-shape property and supplants the ideal $\ (x^2):(x)\subseteq L$. Moreover, we demonstrate that the module $\ M_{(1)}$ serves as a generator for the zero submodule of local cohomology modules $\ Koh_{F}(L)$.

A design where all orders are accepted or rejected is proposed for redispatch markets, leading to a binary outcome for market participants. This design's effectiveness is analyzed through a mathematical model that transforms it into a binary variant. The properties of this model are examined to ensure it makes economic and technically sound sense, and a realistic scenario is presented to test it. The results of this test are evaluated to understand the model's behavior and the implications of the design on procurement practices by the grid operator.

In this study, we examine a specific scenario involving function fields and a particular set of polynomials, concluding that the Galois groups associated with these polynomials mirror a significant aspect of the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture. Our findings build upon a previous result by David, Koutsmeris, and Thorne, and our research implies that the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture holds true for a broad category of polynomials in a specific context. Additionally, our work provides a theoretical framework that can be leveraged to achieve future results related to the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture.

Our research examines the sensitivity of next-generation experiments to identify Higgs boson signals, specifically in searches for the decay process where the Higgs boson produces bottom quark pairs and is accompanied by top quark pair production. We find that current analyses underestimate the Higgs boson signal cross-section by a factor of two to four, which could be mitigated by incorporating top quark pair background suppression techniques. Even with this improvement, we predict that the most sensitive searches for the Higgs boson in experiments like the High Energy Large Anti-lemmas (HEL) and Future Circular Collider (FCC) will have detection limits of 0.5-1.5 times the standard model prediction for the Higgs boson cross-section in future experiments.

To extend the Standard Model, we investigate the possibility of adding a complex scalar doublet with a charge of 1 at the tree level. This additional field is connected to the Higgs boson through an interaction that can be quantified by the ratio $\kappa$, which affects the production and decay rates of the Higgs boson. Specifically, the Higgsstrahlung process, where a Z boson is produced in conjunction with the Higgs boson, is examined to determine if it can reveal evidence of an extended scalar sector even if $\kappa$ is relatively small. To achieve this, we create explicit relationships between $\kappa$ and other parameterizations used in previous analyses. Furthermore, we consider both narrow and broad Z boson resonances to derive these connections. By analyzing the Higgs boson's diphoton decay rate, which has been precisely measured, we can set new constraints on the parameter space related to $\kappa$. Additionally, we determine how many units of $\sigma$ (sigma) are required for the Higgsstrahlung process to significantly exceed its Standard Model counterpart, which occurs when the mass of the complex scalar doublet is around 100 GeV. If this mass is instead around 1 TeV, the process is minimized when $\kappa$ is approximately 0.5, and in this case, the predicted outcome is rather close to the minimum possible value.

While Saturn is ringed by a subtle vortex at its southern pole during summer, the northern pole remains occupied by a persistent and distinctive vortex until the spring equinox. Unlike its southern counterpart, which forms in the spring, the northern vortex exists throughout the summer. This paper examines the composition of the polar stratospheres in both hemispheres using data from the Saturn stratosphere, obtained by the Jupiter Irregular Satellite System Imaging Experiment on the TianGanShui satellite between August and December 2019. By comparing the results from the two hemispheres, it is found that the northern vortex remains isolated by jet streams and retains its purity, whereas the southern vortex loses its purity due to the influx of fast-moving, polar-wide wave patterns. Additionally, this paper explores the recent changes in the Saturnian polar stratosphere and reveals a weakening of the jet streams and vortex layers.

This paper disproves a long-held assumption concerning boundary blow-up for the Schrödinger equation under periodic conditions. Classical evidence supporting the concept of boundary blow-up relies on specific data configurations and specific initial conditions near the boundary. However, when considering the full range of smooth, compactly supported initial conditions, we demonstrate that boundary blow-up is impermissible. Our key argument revolves around the uniform continuity of the solution on the entire domain, a property inherently lost if the solution experiences singularities at the boundary.

This briefing notes on an ongoing project, yet its comprehensive write-up remains to be completed. We're exploring a hypothesis proposed by Bradd Cratchfield and Lars Hultman, which posits that certain $\mathbb F_p$-linear diagonal forms, as defined by Eisenbud, Goto, and Horiegi, are equivalent to $\mathbb F_p$-linear versions of those described by Branson, Huh, and Miller. To date, we've successfully validated this hypothesis for characteristic zero and proved its analogue for positive characteristics, thereby bridging the gap between zero-characteristic and positive-characteristic commutative algebra.

We have developed a holistic understanding of the metal-insulator transition in the two-dimensional Sr$_{2}$NiO$_4$ driven by hydrostatic pressure, which involves strongly correlated electrons at the edge of a band and a balanced effective attraction. Our argument combines empirical observations with theoretical analysis, incorporating $f$-source and background electronic effects as per the LDA+DMFT framework. In this framework, the metal-insulator transition arises from the strong suppression of electronic movements near the edge of the band due to strong correlations. Utilizing spectral weight, we have demonstrated the significance of the motion of electrons in the metal phase and the localized nature of the insulating phase. These results are supported by experiments, showcasing the fundamental role of motion of electrons in this metal-insulator transition and highlighting the fundamental difference between this transition and those driven by filling a gap in a more straightforward scenario.

Quantum dark solitons in a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate have been extensively studied, however the quantum analog of a double dark-soliton, which comprises two coherent holes in a coherent background, lacks current analysis, particularly regarding its early quantum dynamics. Employing quantum hydrodynamics and a mean-field theory based on the Bogoliubov approach, we model this double dark-soliton and reveal its early quantum state characterized by evolving densities and velocities across the soliton domains. We also demonstrate that these features result in a stable quantum double dark-soliton, and upon collision with a quantum dark soliton anti-soliton pair, produces a quantum double soliton instead of a scattering of solitons and oscillations.

This study introduces the notion of a symplectic double vector bundle and its symplectomorphisms, thereby expanding on the concept of a symmetric k-fold vector bundle. We demonstrate that such a structure is equivalent to a symmetric k-fold vector bundle with symmetric multivector fields, satisfying certain properties. Additionally, we establish the relationship between the symplectomorphisms of a symplectic double vector bundle and the linear operators on the underlying k-fold vector bundle. Our work also introduces the concept of Hamiltonian functions and vector fields for a symplectic double vector bundle, leading to the derivation of a Hamiltonian operator for a k-fold vector bundle.

A deep connection between the measures of Kirillov and geometric measures is established for a broad class of orbits in the dual space of a Lie algebra. This investigation involves nilpotent Lie algebras, their conjugacy classes, and the geometric measure's relationship with certain combinatorial constructs known as Carasso's row weights. A central aspect of this research is the discovery of a closed form that encompasses the measures of Kirillov, geometric measures, and the row weights, and can be defined using the Lie derivative in a hypothetical analytic setting. This relationship is examined for various infinite-dimensional, non-associative algebras known as Yangian constructions, revealing that the closed form may no longer be defined on all its conjugacy classes. A distinct class of harmonic measures is then introduced for nilpotent Lie algebras and their conjugacy classes, and a specific harmonic measure is identified for the infinite-dimensional, non-associative algebra known as $U(h_n)$, the Bannu algebra.

A cutting-edge algorithm has been created to accelerate the x-ray scattering experiment data analysis, specifically for energy spectrum reconstruction. This novel method speeds up the process by leveraging a conventional differential filter bank technique, adapting it for complex signals and streamlining the auto-correlation step. As a result, the required optimization steps are significantly reduced, enabling the implementation on high-performance computing platforms and making phase retrieval more accessible for x-ray scattering experiments with spectrometric detection.

We explore how disordered classical statistical mechanics models can be applied to the study of quantum error correcting codes. Focusing on the surface code, we examine its relationship with classical disordered models and demonstrate how the average energy of these classical models is directly linked to the logarithm of the fidelity of the quantum code. This connection allows us to investigate important quantum code properties by leveraging the established techniques of classical statistical mechanics. As an example, we use this approach to find the expected energy of a version of the classical Edwards-Anderson model and relate this outcome to the logarithm of the fidelity of the corresponding quantum surface code. Furthermore, we identify scenarios in which the average energy of classical models exhibits unconventional behaviors that could potentially lead to non-zero thresholds in quantum error correction.

To tackle the challenge of creating a non-trivial gap in tellurene-based quantum wells, we propose using a different material structure - a tellurene/phosphorene/hafniumdioxide superlattice. Our calculations using first-principles methods demonstrate that this structure possesses a noticeable gap despite being chemically inert. Furthermore, we investigate how changing the crystal direction of tellurene or phorphorene through rotation or misorientation can impact the gap, revealing that this change can turn a gapless tellurene into a gapped one. Additionally, we explore the potential of using this design for quantum well devices that can switch between gapless and gapped states through strain application.

This paper offers a modified version of the single-phase flow model in the presence of massive blocks, where we've incorporated a novel approach that diverts flow around blocks through a specific set of curved fronts. These diverted flows are modeled using a modified Dirac-beta function that contributes to a potential theory representation. We've demonstrated that the modified model reduces to the standard block-model representation when fronts are sufficiently straight, and we've established the condition for this limitation to hold. Additionally, we've analyzed the impact of diverting flows on average fluxes and demonstrated that they follow a specific relationship that depends on the geometry of fronts. This result implies that average fluxes may be significant even for highly blocked media, which provides an important counterpoint to conventional views on blocked materials.

The alignment of spin-valve devices can be precisely controlled using a magnetic field due to the distinct magnetic properties of two incorporated materials, one of which is highly resistant to magnetization. When exposed to moderately low exchange fields, these devices exhibit alternative alignment patterns, and our research demonstrates that one of these patterns can be selectively induced through the application of a smaller, opposing field. This discovery enables the enhancement of spin-valve performance at higher temperatures and in the presence of exchange field fluctuations typical of mobile device environments.

In the context of astrophysics, a model is often used to explain observational data and predict outcomes for future observations. The accuracy of these models depends on variables such as stellar masses, black hole spins, and cosmic distances. Determining these variables, known as parameters, is crucial for making informed decisions about future observations and understanding complex astrophysical processes. 

A key challenge arises from the large number of parameters involved, often exceeding ten, which makes conventional methods for exploring model performance and selecting the best hypotheses impractical for complex astrophysical models. Additionally, typical optimization techniques struggle to handle models with a large number of local minima.

To overcome these challenges, a new approach has been developed using a type of utility function that prioritizes the most important parameters and makes the model more manageable for analysis. This approach allows researchers to focus on the most influential parameters and make more informed decisions about future observations.

The utility function approach has several benefits, including the ability to balance experimental resources with computational power and focus on parameters with the greatest impact on future observations. By leveraging advanced computational methods, this approach makes complex astrophysical models accessible for exploration and hypothesis testing.

The utility function approach has significant applications in areas such as binary black hole physics, supernovae theory, and cosmic structure, and is a key component of the GBASE code. This approach enables researchers to develop a deeper understanding of astrophysical processes and make more informed decisions about future observations, thus accelerating the development of new astrophysical

We release a newly annotated dataset called DiscSense, consisting of 1800 sentence pairs, along with associated discourse marker and semantic relation tags. These elements are crucial for understanding the complex meanings behind sentences in a language. Existing research has highlighted the limitations of current models in predicting these elements. Our dataset and a corresponding model, which we have developed, aim to address these limitations. We create a simple classification system that includes multiple categories of discourse markers and semantic relations. The annotation process for DiscSense involved multiple stages and rigorous quality control measures to ensure accuracy. We have also established new evaluation metrics and a corresponding evaluation strategy for the dataset. Our research has also been featured in a previously submitted paper, but we have made significant improvements to the model and have been asked to resubmit our work.

For years, researchers have been attempting to grasp the nature of non-radiative decay in colloidal nanocrystals, with little progress. A significant breakthrough comes in the form of a theoretical framework that incorporates the Mott-Seitz model, revealing its implications on the energy barriers for non-radiative decay. Using this framework, researchers have been able to quantify the energy barriers, which are proportional to (1.26e-0.09)v^2, in units of 10^-19 J, where v represents the velocity of an electron in units of 10^5 m/s. Additionally, this framework demonstrates that the Mott-Seitz model can be applied to nanoscale materials, and it highlights the importance of electron-phonon interactions in determining whether decay is radiative or non-radiative. Further analysis indicates that the Mott-Seitz model can predict the onset of non-radiative decay and suggests that phonon overlap may contribute to the formation of a higher energy barrier in larger nanocrystals.

This paper presents a new training algorithm for neural networks that eliminates the use of intermediate layers. The proposed method alters the error computation method used in backpropagation, doing so in a way that allows neural network connectivity to be optimized through sparse optimization techniques. The new training algorithm is demonstrated to be as effective as traditional training methods, even when neural network connections are highly non-linear, by conducting various experiments using artificial data and real-world image classification datasets.

A classical model is constructed to describe magnetic skyrmions in a toroidal target space. The topology of the target space influences the types of magnetic skyrmions that exist, with only those homotopy classes that correspond to non-trivial cycles in the target space being stable.
